sourceNotes: Seeded from FMS roleplay performance indicators and marketing cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: FMS event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the marketing cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: FDA-published gram amount per food category that fixes the serving declared on the Nutrition Facts panel, so the label's serving is derived from a federal table rather than from package size or what a shopper actually eats.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay judge asks why your store-brand chips show fewer calories per serving than the national brand on the shelf beside them, the defensible answer compares label servings back to the same RACC instead of comparing bag sizes.

terms.definition: Reading shortcut written into FDA labelling guidance: 5% DV or less of a nutrient per serving is low and 20% DV or more is high, which turns the panel's right-hand column into a per-serving screen rather than a per-package one.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a panel and ask whether an item qualifies as a high-fiber or low-sodium choice for a shopper on a dietitian's list; the 5/20 cut points decide the answer, and the values are per serving, so a two-serving package doubles the intake.

terms.definition: Front-of-pack statement about a nutrient's level that is legal only at a defined threshold — "low sodium" at 140 mg or less per serving, "reduced" at 25% less than the reference food, "good source" at 10-19% DV — all measured against the RACC, never the package.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor presenting a new better-for-you line in a buying roleplay will call it 'reduced sodium'; you have to ask which reference food that 25% is measured against before the claim goes on your shelf tag or your circular.

terms.definition: The last day a manufacturer will vouch for peak quality, and the only such date federally regulated in the United States is the one on infant formula — for every other food it is a quality judgment, not a safety deadline or a legal bar to sale.
terms.whyItMatters: When a shopper at the service desk demands a refund on milk one day past the stamp, the defensible response separates the single federally regulated case from the manufacturer's quality date, and store policy takes it from there.

terms.definition: Manufacturer's packing code — plant, line, shift and often a Julian day — printed for the supply chain rather than the shopper, and it is the only marking precise enough to bound which cases a recall actually touches.
terms.whyItMatters: In a recall roleplay the notice names a lot code, not a calendar date; reading the closed code is what keeps you from pulling three weeks of a category off the shelf when only one shift's production is implicated.

terms.definition: Four-step ladder set by percentage of organic ingredients: 100% organic, organic at 95% or more, "made with organic ingredients" at 70-94%, and below 70% only an ingredient-statement mention — and the USDA seal is permitted only on the top two tiers.
terms.whyItMatters: A supplier pitching a 78% organic soup for your natural set cannot carry the seal or front-panel 'organic', and mis-tagging it is a labelling violation you own once it is on your shelf.

terms.definition: Numbering scheme for bulk produce in which a four-digit code marks conventionally grown product and a five-digit code beginning with 9 marks certified organic, so the digit count and the leading 9 decide which ring price the cashier keys.
terms.whyItMatters: Organic apples ringing at the conventional price is a shrink-and-margin leak traced entirely to the wrong PLU, and produce-department roleplays ask you to explain the training fix to a new cashier.

terms.definition: Rotation discipline that ships and shelves by remaining shelf life rather than by receipt order, which diverges from FIFO whenever a later delivery arrives with an earlier expiry — common when a supplier clears its own aging stock.
terms.whyItMatters: Dairy and deli sets are rotated FEFO, and a roleplay on rising perishable shrink usually turns on a clerk who rotated by delivery date and buried a short-dated case behind a fresher one.

terms.definition: Receiving standard written into a supply agreement stating the minimum fraction of total shelf life a delivery must still have at the dock — commonly one-third or 75% — and product below it is refused at delivery, not marked down later.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor arguing that a load of 30-day yogurt with 9 days left is still saleable is asking you to absorb his markdown; quoting the receiving standard is what makes the refusal defensible to your buyer and to the judge.

terms.definition: Loss concentrated in produce, meat, deli and bakery, where spoilage, trim and markdowns typically run 3-6% of department sales against well under 1% in dry grocery — so one storewide shrink target either starves the fresh departments or excuses the center store.
terms.whyItMatters: A store-manager roleplay handing you a 2% shrink goal expects you to set it by department; holding produce to the dry-grocery number forces under-ordering, empty shelves and lost sales that cost more than the shrink saved.

terms.definition: Timed price reduction taken while a short-dated perishable can still sell, sized so the discounted price beats the expected value of holding it — if a $4.00 item has a 40% chance of selling at full price tomorrow, anything above $1.60 today is the better outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: Meat and bakery roleplays hinge on markdown timing: waiting until the final morning converts a partial recovery into a total loss, and the judge wants to hear the discount compared against expected remaining sell-through, not a fixed 50% rule.

terms.definition: Weight removed as fat, bone, rind or wilted outer leaves between the as-purchased case and the saleable package, which raises effective cost per saleable pound: $4.00 per pound bought at a 20% trim rate costs $5.00 per saleable pound.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing a meat or produce cut off the invoice cost is how a department books a margin it never earns; the cutting-test number is what a judge expects behind your retail price on a whole-muscle or whole-melon item.

terms.definition: Case- or pack-level tag whose irreversible color change accumulates exposure over the whole journey, so it reports cumulative abuse rather than the instantaneous reading a probe thermometer gives at the dock.
terms.whyItMatters: A frozen load arriving at spec on the probe can still have thawed and refrozen in transit; the indicator is the evidence that lets you reject the delivery and charge the carrier instead of eating the loss.

terms.definition: Consignment arrangement in which the supplier keeps title to product sitting in the store and is paid only from POS scan data, so the retailer carries no inventory investment and shrink before the scan is the supplier's loss.
terms.whyItMatters: Common in DSD categories like bread and snacks; a vendor-negotiation roleplay turns on who owns the unsold and stolen units, and the answer follows title, which under this arrangement does not transfer until checkout.

terms.definition: Trade funding deducted from the case cost on the purchase invoice itself for a set deal window, which pays on everything bought rather than on anything sold and therefore invites buying far more than the promotion can move.
terms.whyItMatters: A buyer roleplay asks why the manufacturer wants to move you off this structure: the deal was funded on 12 weeks of purchases to support a 2-week ad, and the extra cases either sit or leak into another market.

terms.definition: Trade funding paid after the fact against documented performance — proof of ad, display photos or shipment reports — so the retailer buys at full cost, funds the working capital in the interim, and collects only on what was actually performed.
terms.whyItMatters: Deductions disputes in a vendor roleplay almost always sit here: the retailer claims the ad ran, the supplier says the documentation is short, and the money hangs in accounts receivable until the performance evidence is produced.

terms.definition: Per-unit funding paid on the units that actually scan at the promoted retail during the ad week, which strips out forward-buy incentive entirely because unpurchased-for-promotion inventory earns nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: When you are asked to justify a deeper feature price to a supplier, this is the structure that lets you promise the discount reaches the shopper — every funded unit is a unit that rang at the ad price.

terms.definition: Effect of an order multiple that cannot be broken: a shelf needing 14 units of a 12-count case must take 12 or 24, and on a short-dated perishable the rounded-up half case becomes markdown rather than sales.
terms.whyItMatters: Ordering roleplays on slow perishable SKUs are solved by changing the pack or the delivery frequency, not the order quantity — with a 24-count case and 3 units of weekly movement, the arithmetic guarantees spoilage.

terms.definition: Facings multiplied by units deep, divided by daily unit movement — the number of days a full shelf covers, which is what decides whether a SKU can be replenished on a two-day delivery cycle without going out of stock.
terms.whyItMatters: A shelf holding 18 units against 12 a day covers a day and a half, so a Monday-Thursday delivery schedule empties it every weekend; the fix a judge is listening for is more facings or more deliveries, not a bigger backroom.

terms.definition: The percentage distance held between a store brand and the national brand beside it, typically managed to 15-25%: too narrow and the shopper has no reason to switch, too wide and the shopper reads the store brand as inferior goods.
terms.whyItMatters: Private-label roleplays ask you to reprice an item, and the answer is a gap target with a reason on both sides — the national brand's own promoted price can close the gap to zero during an ad week and stall your own-brand sales.

terms.definition: The lowest-priced item stocked in a category, held below the mainstream store brand and run at a thin or near-zero margin because its job is price image and traffic, with the category's margin recovered on the tier above it.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge challenges you on stocking an item that barely makes money, the defense is architecture: the cheap item anchors the category's price perception and the shoppers it draws trade up within the same set.

terms.definition: The handful of SKUs — milk, eggs, bananas, a leading soda — whose prices shoppers actually remember and use to judge a whole store, which is why they are priced at or below market while unremembered items in the same basket carry the margin.
terms.whyItMatters: A margin-improvement roleplay is failed by raising the price of milk: the price-image items must stay put and the recovery has to come from the items shoppers cannot recall, which is a list you should be able to name.

terms.definition: Item sold at a price per pound on a package of variable actual weight, so cases contain a known count but an unknown total weight and every unit rings a different total at the register.
terms.whyItMatters: Meat, cheese and seafood inventory cannot be valued by case count; a roleplay on department costing expects you to know that receiving records weight, not just cases, or the margin report is fiction.

terms.definition: The job a retailer assigns a category within the store — destination, routine, seasonal or convenience — which sets the metric it is judged on, so a destination category is measured on share and traffic while a convenience category is measured on margin.
terms.whyItMatters: Category-management roleplays start here, because space, price aggressiveness and promotional spend all follow from the role; arguing for more space without naming the role gives the judge nothing to agree with.

terms.definition: Stamp directing the store when to pull an item from the shelf, leaving deliberate remaining life for the shopper at home — it is a stock-rotation instruction to the retailer, not a statement to the consumer about safety.
terms.whyItMatters: Explaining to a shopper who found an item dated tomorrow that the date is aimed at the store and not at them is a routine customer-relations roleplay, and the answer separates rotation from spoilage.

terms.definition: Calendar date printed in plain language for the shopper — sell by, best if used by, use by — as opposed to the manufacturer's coded packing date, and outside infant formula it is voluntary under federal law.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on donating or discounting past-date product depends on knowing these dates are quality guidance rather than a federal expiration, so the store's own policy is what actually governs the decision.

terms.definition: Counts how many separate product lines a company carries, never how many items sit inside them: a grocer running dairy, bakery, and frozen lines has a width of 3 even when those lines hold 400 items between them, while product mix depth counts the items within one line.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix-planning roleplay that asks how a retailer should expand expects width and depth reported as two different counts; answering with adjectives like 'broad' instead of a number loses the indicator.

terms.definition: A brand's own market share divided by the share of its single largest competitor — 20% against a leader's 40% is 0.5x, and only the market leader can score above 1.0 — which is the horizontal axis of the growth-share matrix; two brands holding an identical absolute share therefore land in opposite quadrants depending on how dominant the rival directly above each of them happens to be.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that reports 20% share and calls it strong is answered by asking what the leader holds; the ratio, not the raw percentage, is what drives the portfolio decision.

terms.definition: Amplification of demand variability moving upstream, where a small retail sales swing becomes a larger distributor order swing and a still larger factory order swing, driven by batch ordering, price promotions, forecast updating and shortage gaming — shared point-of-sale data damps it.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays use this to justify sharing real sales data with suppliers, and the four named causes are what turn a vague answer about 'communication' into a scored one.

terms.definition: The theory that exchange rates should adjust until an identical basket of goods costs the same in both countries: if a burger is $5 in the U.S. and £4 in Britain, the implied rate is $1.25 per pound, and a market rate of $1.60 says the pound is overvalued. Trade barriers and non-traded services keep real rates from converging to it.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items give two local prices for one product and ask what the exchange rate implies, or ask why a salary converts to very different living standards in two countries.

terms.definition: Closed-won revenue divided by the number of deals won — $480,000 across 60 wins is $8,000 each. It measures one whole customer agreement, where average order value measures one transaction, so a customer who reorders four times a year raises order count without raising this figure at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking you to justify spending more selling time per account is answered by comparing deal size against cost per sales call, not by citing total revenue.

terms.definition: Failure to exercise reasonable care that results in injury or loss to another.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the most common tort in business and a leading source of liability claims.

terms.definition: The share of respondents picking the top boxes on a satisfaction scale — the 4s and 5s on a 5-point scale, so 380 top-box replies out of 500 is 76%. It measures one transaction immediately after it happens, while the recommend question measures the whole relationship, which is why the two can move in opposite directions in the same month.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items supply raw response counts and expect the top-box percentage; roleplays expect the right survey chosen for a transaction rather than a relationship.

terms.definition: Overestimating both the intensity and the duration of a future emotional reaction; the duration half alone is the durability bias, and the two named causes are focalism -- attending only to the focal event and not to everything else that will fill the day -- and immune neglect, discounting how quickly one rationalizes an outcome. Lottery winners and people newly paralyzed converge far closer than either group predicts.
terms.whyItMatters: A risk-of-personal-decisions item asking whether a competitor should take a demanding promotion is testing this: the answer that survives is one that weighs the ordinary days after the change, not the peak of the reaction to it.

terms.definition: Standards governing the responsible collection, use, protection, and sharing of information.
terms.whyItMatters: Privacy and data-governance dilemmas are common in modern business scenarios.

terms.definition: Revenue times percent margin, minus marketing and sales expense: $10,000,000 at a 40% margin spending $2,500,000 contributes $1,500,000. Unlike marketing ROI it reports dollars added rather than a ratio, so a small program with a spectacular ratio can still contribute less than a large one.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-defense questions ask which of two programs to fund when one has the better return percentage and the other the bigger dollar contribution; the profit line is settled in dollars.

terms.definition: An objective-setting standard requiring an advertising goal to name a measurable communication task, a defined audience, a starting benchmark and a deadline — raise unaided awareness among women 18 to 34 from 20% to 45% within six months — rather than a sales target that advertising alone cannot own.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotional-plan roleplays are frequently scored on whether the stated objective is measurable; a competitor who promises to increase sales has written a goal that no post-campaign study can grade.

terms.definition: Trompenaars' pole opposite universalism: which rule applies depends on the relationship and the circumstance, so a signed contract is a starting point a long-standing partner may reopen, and an obligation to a friend can outrank written policy. Universalist cultures - the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Germany - hold that one standard binds everyone regardless of who is asking, which is why the identical request reads as reasonable flexibility on one side of the table and as favoritism on the other.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay where a long-time distributor asks for terms no other account receives is scored on naming the cultural logic at work before ruling on the request.

terms.definition: The stages a product passes through: introduction, growth, maturity, and decline.
terms.whyItMatters: The stage a product is in drives its marketing, pricing, and distribution.

terms.definition: Holds that a firm should satisfy its target market's wants profitably only in ways that also preserve long-run consumer and social welfare — the third test the plain marketing concept leaves out — so an offering that customers genuinely want and the company profits from can still fail this standard because of the harm it does over time.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions that pit a profitable, popular product against a long-term harm are answered by naming this third test rather than by choosing between customers and profit.

terms.definition: The width of the customer's tolerance divided by six standard deviations of process spread, with Cpk penalizing an off-center mean by measuring only the nearer specification limit; 1.33 is the common minimum and a value below 1.0 means defects are unavoidable even when the process is perfectly stable.
terms.whyItMatters: Supplier-quality roleplays use this figure as the acceptance bar: a supplier can hold a steady process and still fail, which is the argument you make when resolving a quality dispute.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Every open deal multiplied by the win probability its current stage carries, then summed. A $200,000 deal sitting in a 30 percent stage counts as $60,000, so $1.4 million of raw pipeline spread across early stages may weight to under $400,000 — the total becomes a forecast instead of a list of what is theoretically in play.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting items give a table of deal values and stage probabilities and expect the weighted total, not the sum; in a roleplay defending a forecast to a manager, quoting raw pipeline reads as the rookie answer.

terms.definition: An amount subtracted directly from tax owed, so it is worth its full face value — unlike a deduction, which only reduces the income the tax is figured on.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a $1,000 credit with a $1,000 deduction and ask which saves more; the credit does, by the taxpayer's bracket rate.

terms.definition: Satisfaction treated as the gap between what was expected and what was perceived, not as an absolute level of performance — the same 20-minute wait delights a diner quoted 30 minutes and enrages one quoted 10. The operational consequence is that lowering the promise raises satisfaction without changing the kitchen at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Explains a quoted-wait-time or delivery-date decision in a restaurant roleplay far better than any appeal to trying harder.

terms.definition: The ability to understand and manage emotions in yourself and others.
terms.whyItMatters: It underlies teamwork, service, and conflict-resolution answers.

terms.definition: Copies only the blocks changed since the previous backup of any type, so each nightly run is the smallest possible, but restoring requires the last full backup plus every one of these runs applied in order since it — and a single missing or corrupt link breaks the entire chain behind it.
terms.whyItMatters: Records-storage items ask why a company whose nightly job finishes in four minutes still needed nine hours to recover, and the restore chain is the reason.

terms.definition: How a product or brand is perceived in customers' minds relative to competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning shapes differentiation and appeal to the target market.

terms.definition: Communication that informs, persuades, and reminds customers about offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion choices must fit the audience, message, and budget.

terms.definition: A narrow statutory defense allowing an employer to hire on the basis of sex, religion, national origin or age when that characteristic is reasonably necessary to the essence of the business — an actor's sex for a specific role, or a mandatory retirement age for airline pilots. It can never justify a race-based decision, and it differs from business necessity, which defends a neutral rule that happens to screen out a group, whereas this defends an openly stated preference.
terms.whyItMatters: In a staffing roleplay involving a customer preference for one sex, the tested answer is that customer preference is not a valid basis for this defense.

terms.definition: Counts the individual items inside a single line -- sizes, flavors, formulations, models: a toothpaste line of 4 flavors in 3 tube sizes is 12 items deep, and adding a fifth flavor deepens the mix without widening it, because width counts lines alone.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a table of lines and items and ask for one number; students who add every item in the company report the length instead of the depth of the line asked about.

terms.definition: Invitations sent per existing user multiplied by the share of those invitations that convert into new users — 5 invites at a 25% conversion rate gives k = 1.25 — where any value above 1.0 compounds into self-sustaining growth and any value below 1.0 produces a decaying series that halts on its own once paid acquisition stops, so the threshold is exactly 1.0 and not merely 'high'.
terms.whyItMatters: A referral-program roleplay is scored on stating the break-even threshold and the two inputs you would change to reach it, not on calling the campaign shareable.

terms.definition: Unit price plus freight, insurance, duties and tariffs, customs brokerage, and handling to the receiving dock — the total that makes an offshore quote comparable to a domestic one, which is why the lower quoted unit price frequently loses once every downstream charge is added.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays present a cheaper overseas bid and expect you to reject a comparison based on quoted price alone by adding the delivery-related charges before deciding.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: Purchase price plus installation, training, consumables, maintenance and downtime across the asset's life, minus its resale value — so a $12,000 machine burning $400 of supplies a year beats a $9,000 machine burning $1,600 within five years. It answers a price objection by moving the comparison from acquisition price to lifetime cost.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer says a competitor quoted less, judges look for this calculation rather than a discount, because conceding on price is the response the rubric marks down.

terms.definition: State-granted legal permission to perform work that is illegal without it — signing an audit opinion, selling securities, practicing law. A voluntary certification is issued by a private association instead, so losing it costs you the letters after your name but never the legal right to keep working.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay that asks what a new hire may and may not sign turns on this line: an unlicensed staff accountant can prepare the workpapers but cannot issue the opinion.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.term: Goleman's four-domain model of emotional intelligence
terms.definition: Sorts emotional competence into four domains — self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, relationship management — arranged as a 2x2 grid: the left column is personal competence (handling yourself), the right column is social competence (handling others), the top row is recognition and the bottom row is regulation. It is a mixed model of learnable workplace competencies, so it is assessed with a 360-degree rater inventory rather than with a right-answer test.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that lists four manager behaviors and asks which one is social awareness rather than relationship management is scored against this grid, and a management roleplay judge expects a candidate to name which domain a weakness sits in before proposing the fix.

terms.definition: Copies everything changed since the last full backup, so Friday's run is far larger than Monday's, but a restore needs exactly two pieces — the full backup plus the newest run — against the incremental approach's full backup plus every intervening night in sequence.
terms.whyItMatters: A business-continuity roleplay trades nightly window against recovery speed, and the graded answer is which of these two schemes buys the shorter restore.

terms.definition: Two towns pull trade from the countryside between them in proportion to their populations and in inverse proportion to the square of the distance to each; the indifference line sits at the miles between them ÷ (1 + the square root of the larger town's population divided by the smaller town's), measured out from the smaller town, and households past that line shop the larger one.
terms.whyItMatters: A trading-area item on the marketing exam gives two populations and the miles between the towns and expects the boundary mileage as a number; in a site-selection roleplay it is how you defend where a store stops drawing customers instead of waving at a map.

terms.definition: Reach multiplied by average frequency, the one number that sizes a schedule's total weight: 40% of the target seen four times is 160. The same 160 can be bought as 80% reach at 2.0 frequency, which is why the figure alone never describes a schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-planning items hand the competitor a reach figure and a frequency figure and ask for the schedule's weight, or give the weight and one factor and ask for the other; a roleplay defending a media plan to a client is expected to state both halves, not just the total.

terms.definition: The view that managers owe duties to every group affected by the firm — employees, customers, suppliers, communities, and lenders as well as owners; it opposes Friedman's shareholder primacy doctrine, which holds that a manager's sole social responsibility is increasing owner returns within the rules of the game.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics roleplays about closing a profitable plant are scored on naming both positions and defending the recommendation against the other one.

terms.definition: A group of related products sold under one brand or category.
terms.whyItMatters: Line decisions balance customer choice against cost and complexity.

terms.definition: Environmental marketing claims the seller cannot substantiate, policed in the United States by the FTC's Green Guides at 16 CFR Part 260, which treat unqualified general claims such as 'eco-friendly' or 'green' as deceptive because they imply every possible environmental benefit, and require a degradability claim to mean complete breakdown within one year of customary disposal; a truthful narrow claim must therefore be stated narrowly to be lawful.
terms.whyItMatters: Sustainability roleplays that ask you to approve a packaging claim are scored on naming the standard and qualifying the claim, since an unqualified benefit statement is a legal exposure, not just a marketing choice.

terms.definition: An international quality-management standard certifying that documented processes exist, are followed and are audited by an independent registrar with surveillance visits — it certifies the management SYSTEM, not the product, so a registered firm can lawfully make a mediocre item consistently.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays treat registration as evidence of process discipline, and the judge is listening for the caveat that it guarantees consistency rather than excellence.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: Ramped headcount times individual quota times the attainment rate the team really achieves — 20 reps carrying $500,000 each but hitting 70 percent supports $7 million of revenue, not the $10 million the quota sheet implies. Skipping the attainment factor is what makes a hiring plan promise revenue the team has never once delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: A growth-planning roleplay that asks how many reps to hire to reach a revenue goal is graded on multiplying in historical attainment; the exam tests it as a three-factor calculation.

terms.definition: Spending the promotional budget ON THE CHANNEL — trade allowances, dealer incentives, training and sales calls — so intermediaries stock and sell the line to shoppers who arrived with no preference. A pull strategy spends the same money on END CONSUMERS instead, so demand arrives at the store and forces the retailer to carry the item. Push is typical for low-differentiation and business-to-business goods; pull requires enough advertising weight to move consumers first.
terms.whyItMatters: Coordinating channel management with marketing activity is directly tested, and roleplays ask which way to aim a limited promotional budget for a product no consumer has heard of.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: A situation where two or more moral principles conflict and demand judgment.
terms.whyItMatters: Recognizing and resolving dilemmas is central to leadership and compliance.

terms.definition: The mathematical examination of data to identify patterns, test relationships, and support decisions.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors are tested on interpreting findings and drawing evidence-based conclusions.

terms.definition: Estimates the probability a shopper in a neighborhood picks one particular store as that store's selling area ÷ travel time raised to a decay exponent (commonly 2), divided by the same ratio summed across every competing store; multiplying that probability by neighborhood households and their annual category spending turns it into a sales forecast for the site.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-comparison questions that ask which of three locations captures the most volume are solved by ranking size-over-distance-squared ratios, and unlike a single breaking-point line this one gives every store a share of every neighborhood — the distinction a judge probes.

terms.definition: The blend of advertising, publicity, sales promotion, and personal selling.
terms.whyItMatters: A mix lets competitors recommend more than one communication path.

terms.definition: Failing to reject a null hypothesis that is in fact false, so a real difference exists and the test misses it; its probability is beta, power equals 1 minus beta, and a study planned at the conventional 0.80 power still misses a true effect 20 percent of the time. A Type I error is the opposite mistake, calling a difference real when it is not.
terms.whyItMatters: When a research write-up reports no difference between two package designs and the exam asks which project error was made, the answer is the missed-effect error, and it is the one an undersized sample causes.

terms.definition: Total number of items across every line the firm sells, equal to width multiplied by average depth: 5 lines averaging 8 items each gives a length of 40, so a company can lengthen its mix without widening it by adding items to lines it already runs.
terms.whyItMatters: Product-mix questions hand you width and average depth and expect the multiplication; a roleplay judge scoring a merchandising plan looks for the total item count you commit the buyer to carrying.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: A control that releases payment only when the purchase order, the receiving report and the supplier invoice agree on item, quantity and price; any one document alone can be forged or wrong, so requiring all three is what blocks payment for goods never ordered or never delivered.
terms.whyItMatters: Accounts-payable and ethics-in-purchasing roleplays ask what stops a fraudulent invoice from being paid, and naming all three documents plus the fields compared is the complete answer.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: Diagnosing the buyer's problem through questioning and recommending the right fit even when that means a smaller order, as against transactional selling, which moves a known item at speed and treats the exchange as complete at the register. The dividing line is who defines the need: the buyer arrives with it in a transaction, the rep uncovers it here.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay customer asks for a product that will not solve their stated problem, the rubric credits the competitor who redirects the recommendation over the one who rings up the request.

terms.definition: Using prices like $9.99 to shape customer perception of value.
terms.whyItMatters: It shows how price presentation affects customer behavior and sales.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: Treats emotional intelligence as a genuine intelligence with four ranked branches — perceiving emotion, using emotion to facilitate thinking, understanding how emotions combine and change, and managing emotion — and measures it with the MSCEIT, a maximum-performance test whose items are scored against consensus or expert norms instead of asking a person to rate themselves.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam questions that contrast the two dominant EI frameworks turn on this: this one is an ability test with scoreable answers, while the competency model is a rated inventory of habits, and picking the wrong one loses the item.

terms.definition: A 99.999% uptime commitment, which permits roughly 5.3 minutes of unplanned downtime across an entire year; each nine dropped multiplies that allowance by ten, so 99.99% permits about 53 minutes, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, and 99% about 3.65 days — which is why a vendor's extra decimal costs so much.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay compares two hosting quotes whose uptime promises differ by one decimal, and converting each into annual minutes is what makes the price gap defensible.

terms.definition: A distinctive strength that lets a business outperform its competitors.
terms.whyItMatters: Naming the advantage shapes marketing messages and differentiation.

terms.definition: Rating points counted only against the demographic actually being bought instead of against every household in the market, so a broad-appeal buy delivering 200 gross rating points may deliver just 60 of these if only 30% of its viewers fall inside the target.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item that shows a schedule looking strong on total weight but thin on the buying demographic is testing this distinction, and a media-plan roleplay that quotes only the gross figure to a client buying an 18-to-34 audience has hidden the waste.

terms.definition: Law developed through court decisions and legal precedents rather than legislation.
terms.whyItMatters: Many business principles, like contract formation, are rooted in common law.

terms.definition: Building a company's overall reputation and identity across its offerings.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong corporate branding creates loyalty and justifies premium pricing.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.term: Hazard analysis and critical control points
terms.definition: A seven-principle food-safety system that analyzes biological, chemical and physical hazards, fixes the specific steps where a hazard can be eliminated or controlled, sets a measurable critical limit at each such step, then monitors, corrects, verifies and records — control at those points, not final-product testing, is what proves safety.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about food handling reward naming the control step and its measurable limit — a cooking temperature or a holding time — instead of general cleanliness advice.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Count of deals where the buyer bought nothing at all, divided by all closed-lost deals — not by all opportunities. If 60 of 100 losses were no-decisions, the problem is urgency and the business case, because a buyer who chose a rival was at least persuaded to purchase; splitting losses this way points at two completely different fixes.
terms.whyItMatters: A win-loss review roleplay is scored on separating the two loss types before recommending anything, and the exam plants a competitor-versus-status-quo distinction in the stem.

terms.definition: The identity and reputation a person projects through their online presence.
terms.whyItMatters: A personal social media brand can boost or damage credibility.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Emotional self-perception measured as a personality disposition: instruments such as the TEIQue ask a person to agree or disagree with statements about themselves across roughly fifteen facets, so the score records self-belief and overlaps heavily with the Big Five. Ability EI, by contrast, is scored on correct answers to emotion problems, which is why the two kinds of measure correlate only weakly with each other.
terms.whyItMatters: A human resources roleplay in which a candidate proposes an EI screen for hiring is judged on knowing that a self-report inventory can be gamed by an applicant while a performance test cannot.

terms.definition: A cloud arrangement where the provider runs the hardware, storage and virtualization while the customer still patches the operating system and everything stacked above it; platform services shift that operating system and runtime to the provider, and software as a service leaves the customer responsible for nothing but their own data and user settings.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks who is at fault when an unpatched server is breached, and the answer depends entirely on which of these three lines the contract drew.

terms.definition: Weights availability by the share of category dollar volume rung up in the stores that stock an item rather than the share of stores stocking it: 400 supermarkets out of 2,000 can be 65% ACV when they are the busiest 400, so an item in a fifth of outlets can still stand in front of two-thirds of category purchasing power.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution items hand a store count alongside a volume weighting and expect the weighted figure; a marketing-plan roleplay that claims 'we reach most of the market' collapses when the judge asks which of the two numbers that claim rests on.

terms.definition: Paid, nonpersonal communication delivered through media to large audiences.
terms.whyItMatters: Advertising builds broad brand awareness efficiently and at scale.

terms.definition: Profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price, taxable only once the sale happens and taxed at a lower rate when the asset was held over a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios ask whether a client owes tax on a stock that has risen in value; unrealized gains are not taxed until sold.

terms.definition: Adds a new size, flavor, color, or form under an existing brand inside the category it already competes in; a brand extension instead carries that brand into a different category -- a cherry version of a cola is the first, a cola-branded snack chip is the second.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays ask you to grow a brand without new advertising weight; naming the wrong one of the pair gives away that you cannot tell same-category growth from category entry.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: A company-wide philosophy making every employee responsible for continuous improvement and customer-defined quality; quality assurance is the narrower set of process activities designed to prevent defects, and quality control is the narrowest — the inspection and testing that finds defects after production.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items line up the three terms and ask which one an inspection station belongs to; sorting philosophy from prevention from detection is the whole question.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: A short-window, fixed-dollar bonus paid per unit on one targeted product — $50 a unit for 30 days, frequently funded by the manufacturer and paid outside the regular commission plan. An accelerator instead lifts the commission percentage on everything sold past quota, so one steers which item gets pushed and the other rewards total volume.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selling items describe a vendor paying a retailer's floor staff per unit and ask what the payment is; a promotion roleplay expects you to name the mechanism that redirects selling effort to one slow-moving SKU.

terms.definition: A contract term requiring bargaining-unit employees to join the union or pay fees as a condition of continued employment — a union shop allows a grace period of 30 days after hire, shortened to 7 days in construction. Section 14(b) of the Taft-Hartley Act lets a state outlaw such clauses entirely, which is what a right-to-work state does, leaving the union obligated to represent employees who pay nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A labor-relations roleplay set in a right-to-work state is scored on knowing the clause is unenforceable there while the duty of fair representation continues.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Respecting and adapting to the values and practices of different cultures.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets a business serve diverse markets and build inclusive teams.

terms.definition: The computational discovery of patterns and correlations hidden in large datasets.
terms.whyItMatters: Mining surfaces competitive insights that simple reports would miss.

terms.definition: Counts the plain percentage of outlets in the defined universe that stock an item — 400 of 2,000 stores is 20% — and says nothing about how much those outlets sell; dividing weighted (%ACV) coverage by this number gives a quality-of-distribution ratio that runs above 1.0 when the item sits in the bigger stores and below it when the item is stranded in small ones.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-choice questions supply both coverage figures and ask which distribution plan is stronger; the ratio between them is the answer, and treating the two numbers as interchangeable is the classic miss on that item.

terms.definition: One percent of all the households or people in a market's universe, counted whether or not their set is switched on, so a program watched by 90,000 homes in a 1,500,000-household market rates 6.0.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-per-point math on the marketing exam starts here, and competitors lose the item by treating the figure as a share of viewers rather than a percent of the whole market.

terms.definition: FINRA registration permitting an individual to sell general securities to the public, earned by passing the Securities Industry Essentials exam plus a top-off exam and requiring sponsorship by a member firm — a candidate cannot even sit for it unaffiliated. Charging a fee for advice rather than selling products requires a Series 65 or 66 instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services roleplay that asks what a new advisor may do on day one hinges on which registration is in place and who sponsored it.

terms.definition: Adds items between price or feature points a line already covers, usually to close a gap a rival occupies -- dropping a $600 model between the existing $450 and $850 units; line stretching instead pushes the line past the top or bottom of its current range.
terms.whyItMatters: A merchandising roleplay that reports a competitor winning a mid-price slot is scored on filling the gap rather than repricing the whole line.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.

terms.definition: An energy-control procedure requiring every power source to a machine to be isolated, physically locked, and tagged by the individual servicing it — with the rule that only that person may remove their own lock — so no one can restart equipment while a colleague is inside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment-safety roleplays about a maintenance injury expect this named procedure and the one-worker-one-lock rule, not general advice to turn the machine off.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: Quantifying the buyer's gain in the buyer's own numbers — hours saved times loaded labor rate, or scrap avoided times unit cost — so the proposal shows a payback period instead of a feature list. Feature-benefit selling states what a feature does for the customer; this states what that outcome is worth in dollars per year.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business roleplays that give you the client's volumes and costs are asking for a dollar case, and a competitor who only lists benefits leaves the quantified point unscored.

terms.definition: A court doctrine presuming that directors who acted on an informed basis, in good faith, and without personal interest are shielded from liability even when the decision loses money; the presumption is rebutted by showing gross negligence or self-dealing, not by showing a bad outcome.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why a board is not liable for a failed acquisition, and the tested point is that the doctrine reviews the decision process rather than the result.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: Maps five ways of handling a disagreement — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating — on two axes: assertiveness, meaning concern for your own outcome, and cooperativeness, meaning concern for the other party's. Collaborating is high on both and costs the most time; compromising sits at the middle of both and splits the difference, so treating those two as synonyms is the classic wrong answer.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict roleplays name a deadline, and the judge wants the mode matched to it — collaborate when the relationship and the outcome both matter and time exists, compromise when it does not.

terms.definition: The final digit of a code such as a twelve-digit UPC, computed from the digits before it so a scanner can catch its own misread: multiply the digits in odd positions by three, add the digits in even positions, and choose the last digit that lifts the total to the next multiple of ten.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-records questions ask how a scanner knows a keyed-in barcode was mistyped without any lookup, and this arithmetic is the mechanism.

terms.definition: The specific actions and tools used to carry out a marketing strategy.
terms.whyItMatters: Tactics turn strategy into concrete, executable actions.

terms.definition: Short-term incentives like coupons, contests, and discounts that spur purchases.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotions drive quick sales, trial, and inventory clearance.

terms.definition: The share of each order a platform keeps, generally 8 to 20 percent of gross merchandise value plus a fixed per-item charge, deducted before the seller is paid: a $50 order at 15 percent plus $0.99 nets the seller $41.51 before shipping and returns. Whether the channel is viable depends on that net landing above the seller's fully loaded cost, not on the headline price.
terms.whyItMatters: Entrepreneurship and channel roleplays comparing a marketplace to an owned web store are scored on netting the take rate out before comparing the two channels' contribution.

terms.definition: How a product is differentiated in the market and in customers' minds.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear positioning conveys unique value and targets the right segments.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: Outsourcing physical distribution functions — warehousing, transportation, freight handling — to a provider that owns trucks and buildings; a fourth-party provider owns no assets and instead manages the other providers, acting as a single coordinating layer over several third parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution-strategy questions ask which outsourcing level fits a firm that lacks not trucks but the ability to coordinate several carriers, and the asset-owning versus orchestrating split is the answer.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: The FTC rule confining outbound sales calls to a residence to the hours between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. in the customer's local time zone, and requiring the caller to state who is calling, what is being sold and the total cost before taking any payment. A New York center dialing California at 8:30 p.m. Eastern is legal because the customer's clock reads 5:30 p.m.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items plant a two-time-zone call and ask whether it is lawful, which is decided by the customer's local hour; an outbound-calling roleplay expects the disclosure sequence before any card number is requested.

terms.definition: Summary measures such as averages and percentages that describe collected data.
terms.whyItMatters: They translate raw data into insights that justify strategy choices.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: Divides what is known about a person into four panes by crossing known-to-self against known-to-others: open, blind, hidden and unknown. Asking for feedback shrinks the blind pane, while voluntary self-disclosure shrinks the hidden pane — the two moves are not interchangeable, and only the first can surface a habit you cannot see in yourself.
terms.whyItMatters: A written item asking which pane a manager reduces by running a 360-degree review, and roleplays that ask a competitor to assess personal strengths and weaknesses, both depend on separating feedback from disclosure.

terms.definition: Normalization's opening stage: every column holds one indivisible value and no table repeats a group of columns across a single row (no phone1, phone2, phone3). It removes repeating groups and nothing else — a partial dependency on part of a composite key survives it, and a transitive dependency survives both it and the second stage.
terms.whyItMatters: A database item hands the competitor a customer table with three comma-packed phone columns and asks which normal form it breaks; the answer is the first, and answering the third throws the point away.

terms.definition: Divides a brand's sales by its %ACV coverage so brands with unequal shelf presence can be compared on equal footing: $2,000,000 on 40% ACV is $50,000 per point and beats $3,000,000 on 90% ACV at $33,333 per point, which says the smaller brand has earned more distribution rather than more advertising.
terms.whyItMatters: A marketing-plan defense that has to say where the next dollar goes is decided by which brand turns each point of coverage into the most volume; the exam version simply hands sales and coverage and asks for the per-point figure.

terms.definition: The percentage of sets actually in use that are tuned to a given program, so a show rating 6 in a market where only half the sets are on carries a 12 — the figure is always larger than the program's own rating because its denominator is smaller.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a rating and this figure for the same program and ask which one a national advertiser should buy against; the answer is the rating, because only it is measured against the full market a campaign is paying to cover.

terms.definition: Selling price minus variable cost per unit - the dollars each extra sale releases to cover fixed costs and then profit. Gross profit per unit subtracts the full cost of goods sold instead, charging the unit for fixed manufacturing cost that this measure deliberately leaves out.
terms.whyItMatters: Every break-even item on the finance exam needs this figure first, and a competitor who reaches for gross profit computes a break-even volume that is too high.

terms.definition: Extends a line beyond the price range it now serves -- downward into cheaper segments, upward into premium ones, or both at once, as when a marque starting at $30,000 adds a $19,000 entry car; line filling by contrast stays entirely inside the range already covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Positioning roleplays warn about trading down: stretching downward risks the parent brand's image, and judges look for that risk named alongside the volume it buys.

terms.definition: Assigns every small geographic unit — a ZIP+4 or a census block group of roughly 100 to 200 households — to a lifestyle cluster by joining census demographics to purchase data, on the assumption that neighbors buy alike; Nielsen's PRIZM sorts U.S. neighborhoods into 68 such clusters, so media and direct mail are bought against a cluster code rather than against an age band.
terms.whyItMatters: Site-selection and direct-mail roleplays reward naming the cluster system and the unit it works at; saying 'we will target that ZIP code' without the cluster logic reads as guessing.

terms.definition: A structured visit by managers to the actual place work happens, to observe the process and ask questions rather than to inspect people or correct anyone on the spot — the no-blame, observe-only rule is what keeps workers from staging the process for the visitor.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a manager should diagnose a slow process, the expected answer is direct observation at the work site rather than a report or a meeting, which is what an operations judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: Placing the product in the customer's hands for a free trial, test drive or home-approval period and letting possession persuade, because giving the item back later registers as a loss. A takeaway close works from the opposite direction, threatening to withdraw the offer or the model rather than handing it over.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail and automotive roleplays with a hesitant buyer reward a named trial-based close, and pairing it with the store's return policy shows you know the company's selling rules.

terms.definition: A symbol, word, or phrase that identifies and distinguishes a business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brands are valuable assets; competitors must understand trademark protection and infringement.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Techniques to address disagreements and reach mutually acceptable solutions.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong conflict resolution keeps teams cohesive and prevents escalation.

terms.definition: A structured request that filters and retrieves specific information from a database.
terms.whyItMatters: Querying lets competitors pull exactly the data they need instead of sifting everything.

terms.definition: Measurable population traits such as age, income, education, and location.
terms.whyItMatters: Demographics let a business tailor marketing to specific segments.

terms.definition: Direct, person-to-person communication to inform, persuade, and build relationships.
terms.whyItMatters: It enables customized pitches and problem-solving for high-value sales.

terms.definition: A gesture carrying a fixed verbal translation that works with no speech at all - a thumbs-up, a head shake, the finger-and-thumb ring - which is precisely what separates it from an illustrator, a gesture that means nothing apart from the words it accompanies, such as sketching a package's size in the air. Because the translation is assigned by culture rather than by resemblance, this type can invert across a border: the same ring means money in Japan and is obscene in Brazil.
terms.whyItMatters: An international roleplay that has you demonstrate a product to a foreign buyer is scored on choosing gestures whose meaning does not flip, and exam items ask which gesture type still communicates when used silently.

terms.definition: Creating a distinct name, symbol, and image for a specific offering.
terms.whyItMatters: Product branding helps customers identify and prefer that offering.

terms.definition: Sorts U.S. adults into eight consumer types on two axes — primary motivation (ideals, achievement or self-expression) and level of resources and innovation — with Innovators at the top of the resource axis and Survivors at the bottom; it classifies the individual from a survey instrument, whereas PRIZM classifies the neighborhood from census and purchase data, so the two cannot be used interchangeably.
terms.whyItMatters: When a judge asks which segmentation system you would buy, naming VALS and stating its two axes shows you know the difference between a person-level and a household-level system.

terms.definition: A solicitation that describes a problem and invites vendors to propose their own solution, approach and price, evaluated on weighted criteria beyond cost — where a request for quotation specifies the exact item and quantity already and asks only for price and delivery, making it a lowest-bidder instrument.
terms.whyItMatters: Bid-process roleplays turn on choosing the right document: asking for solutions when you already know the specification wastes vendor effort, and asking only for price on an undefined need produces incomparable bids.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: Sellers must re-scrub their calling lists against the federal registry at least every 31 days, and may reach a listed consumer only through an existing business relationship — 18 months after that person's last purchase, or 3 months after an inquiry — or with signed written permission. A list bought once and used for a year fails the scrub requirement no matter how it was sourced.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give a purchase date and a call date and ask whether the relationship exemption still covers the call; a prospecting roleplay is scored on saying how often the list is cleaned.

terms.definition: How easily an asset can be converted to cash without losing much value.
terms.whyItMatters: Liquidity explains why a profitable business can still run short of cash.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation until the required feeling is genuinely experienced, so expression and emotion match — as against surface acting, where a smile is layered over an unchanged feeling. The two produce the same visible behavior with opposite costs, because it is the mismatch inside surface acting, not the effort of acting, that drives exhaustion.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching roleplays where a supervisor must help a frustrated employee face the public are graded on teaching the employee to reframe the customer's motive rather than just ordering a better face.

terms.definition: The stage requiring every non-key column to depend on the whole composite key rather than on one piece of it — a table keyed on (order_id, product_id) that also stores the customer's name breaks it, because the name follows order_id alone. It does nothing whatever when the key is a single column, since a one-column key has no part to depend on.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a table already in first normal form, an exam item asks what still has to be split out; only the partial-dependency test tells the competitor which columns move to a new table.

terms.definition: Forecasts a new brand's settled share as cumulative penetration × repeat-purchase rate × buying-rate index — 40% × 25% × 1.2 = 12% share — so a launch that everybody tries and nobody buys twice collapses on the middle term no matter how large the trial figure looks in the panel data.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product forecast items give the three panel figures and expect the multiplied share; in a plan presentation the same arithmetic is what separates a trial problem, which advertising can fix, from a repeat problem, which only the product can.

terms.definition: The number of exposures needed inside a single purchase cycle before a message registers at all — below it the spend is wasted and above it the spend is redundant. The working planning standard is three exposures, from Krugman's three-hit theory.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client wants the budget spread over more vehicles is a test of this: adding vehicles raises reach but can drop everyone below three exposures, leaving a campaign that technically touched the market and communicated nothing.

terms.definition: The set of unwritten mutual expectations between employer and worker — promotion prospects, schedule flexibility, job security, loyalty — that no signed document records but both sides act on. Breaching it, such as quietly ending remote work after implying it was permanent, damages trust and drives resignations even when nothing legally binding was broken.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay describes an angry workforce after a policy change that violated no written rule, this is the concept that names what actually went wrong.

terms.definition: Cuts slow items from a line by ranked contribution rather than by unit volume, acting on the common finding that the bottom half of a catalog produces under 5% of sales; the deciding test is what share of a cut item's buyers switch to a surviving item instead of to a rival.
terms.whyItMatters: An assortment roleplay hands you a sales-by-item list; the winning answer cuts on contribution and states the transfer assumption, because a high-volume item can carry almost no margin.

terms.definition: The way customers decide what, when, where, and why to purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding buying-behavior factors lets competitors target the right message and offer.

terms.definition: Assigning each item a storage location based on picking velocity, unit weight and case cube, so the fastest-moving lines sit closest to packing at waist height — the objective is minimizing picker travel distance, which is the largest single component of order-fulfillment labor.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about slow order fulfillment expect a layout answer tied to pick frequency, not more staff, and the travel-time argument is what makes it persuasive.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: Total pay a rep receives at exactly 100% of quota — base salary plus variable pay at plan, so a $60,000 base with $60,000 of commission at plan is $120,000 at a 50/50 pay mix. It is a plan figure and not a promise: only the base half is paid regardless of results, which is what separates it from a salary.
terms.whyItMatters: A recruiting roleplay that pitches a sales job is scored on explaining the split honestly, and quoting the total as if it were guaranteed is an ethical mark against you.

terms.definition: Renewal credit a credentialed professional must earn on a fixed cycle to keep the credential active — most state boards require a CPA to report 120 hours across a rolling three-year period with a 20-hour annual floor plus a mandated ethics course, and unused hours lapse rather than carry forward. Unlike a degree, it has no completion point.
terms.whyItMatters: The finance roleplay that asks how an accountant stays qualified year to year wants the cycle and the hour count, not a sentence about lifelong learning.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation before the emotion peaks so that the feeling itself changes — an antecedent-focused move, as opposed to expressive suppression, which lets the feeling run and hides only the outward signal. Suppression is the costlier of the pair: it consumes attention, degrades memory of the conversation, and leaves internal arousal untouched.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking which self-control tactic preserves a manager's recall of a hostile meeting expects reappraisal, and roleplays on composure reward reframing over a clenched poker face.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: Multiplies target households × awareness % × trial % × availability (%ACV) × repeat % × units bought per repeat buyer to reach a first-year volume, so a chain of five decimals well below 1.0 shrinks 10,000,000 households into a few hundred thousand units, and each factor names a different budget line that has to be funded to move it.
terms.whyItMatters: Concept-test forecast questions supply the five percentages and expect the unit answer; walking the chain aloud is also how a plan defends why awareness money and distribution money are not substitutes for each other.

terms.definition: Activities that build positive relationships with the public and media.
terms.whyItMatters: PR manages image, trust, and credibility through third-party voices.

terms.definition: The 2002 federal statute passed after the Enron and WorldCom collapses that makes the CEO and CFO personally certify the accuracy of financial reports under Section 302, requires management assessment of internal controls over financial reporting under Section 404, and protects employees who report fraud.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items about why a public company's managers must sign off on control testing name this statute, and the section numbers distinguish the certification duty from the controls duty.

terms.definition: Methods such as brainstorming and focus groups used to create product concepts.
terms.whyItMatters: Structured idea generation yields higher-quality innovations.
