terms.definition: A candidate group qualifies as a market segment only if it passes five named tests — measurable (its size and buying power can be quantified), substantial (large and profitable enough to serve alone), accessible (reachable through some channel or medium), differentiable (it responds differently from other segments to a change in the mix) and actionable (the firm can actually build and run a program for it); failing any one of the five makes it a description of people, not a segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Market-planning roleplays that ask you to defend a chosen segment are scored on running it against the criteria out loud; the segment competitors usually pick fails 'substantial' or 'accessible'.

terms.definition: An INTERNAL request from a department asking purchasing to buy something, carrying no commitment to any outside party; the purchase order that purchasing then issues is the EXTERNAL document, and it is the offer that forms a binding contract when the supplier accepts it.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchasing-control questions ask which document a department head signs and which one legally obligates the company; treating the internal request as the order is the standard error.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: Federal law requiring prior express written consent — signed, specific to marketing contact, and not made a condition of buying anything — before an autodialer or prerecorded message may call or text a mobile number, and requiring every seller to keep its own internal do-not-call list for five years. A checkbox buried in a purchase flow does not meet the standard.
terms.whyItMatters: A digital-selling roleplay on texting a prospect list is graded on whether you ask how consent was captured; exam items contrast a consumer who bought something with one who signed a marketing permission.

terms.definition: The retailer issues a purchase order, TAKES TITLE to the goods, sets its own retail price, carries the inventory risk, and owns the customer record and the return. In a third-party marketplace relationship the seller keeps title and sets price while the platform merely lists and collects a commission — so the seller keeps control and the margin but also the unsold stock, and the platform, not the seller, may hold the buyer's data.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-selection roleplays for an online launch turn on who owns the customer relationship afterward, which decides whether the brand can remarket to those buyers at all.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: The ability to discuss and reach agreements that satisfy multiple parties.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation determines outcomes in sales, contracts, and partnerships.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: Paid media spend divided by net sales, times 100, then benchmarked against the category norm — a 3% ratio in a category averaging 8% flags underinvestment. It counts media only, so it always reads lower than the marketing expense ratio for the same plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Plan-review questions supply a company ratio and an industry average and ask whether spending is adequate; the comparison, not the raw number, is what earns the point.

terms.definition: The share of the target exposed at or above the threshold number of times — conventionally three or more — so a schedule with 70% total reach may deliver only 35% of this, because the half of the audience that saw the ad once or twice does not count toward it.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-plan items give a reach curve and a frequency distribution and ask which of two schedules performs better; the one with lower total reach usually wins because more of its audience cleared the three-exposure threshold.

terms.definition: Probability that a test detects an effect that really is there, computed as 1 minus beta, with 0.80 the planning convention that accepts a one-in-five chance of missing a true difference; it rises with a larger sample, a larger true effect, and a looser alpha, which is why sample size is chosen before data collection, not after.
terms.whyItMatters: A sampling-plan roleplay that asks how many respondents are enough is answered by the effect worth detecting and the power target, not by a round number like 100.

terms.definition: Cuts promotion, development, and service spending on a declining item toward zero while continuing to sell it, milking cash from the buyers who remain; divestment instead sells or discontinues the item outright, freeing shelf space and capital at once but ending that cash stream immediately.
terms.whyItMatters: Life-cycle roleplays put a fading item in front of you and score whether you choose between milking it and killing it, with a reason tied to remaining loyal demand.

terms.definition: The blend of product, price, place, and promotion used to reach a target market.
terms.whyItMatters: The four Ps are the standard framework for building a marketing recommendation.

terms.definition: A supplier-provided document in a fixed sixteen-section order under the Globally Harmonized System, covering hazards, handling, exposure controls, first aid and disposal — the fixed section order is the point, because a responder finds first-aid information in the same place on every sheet.
terms.whyItMatters: A chemical-spill roleplay expects you to say where the handling and first-aid instructions live and that the sheets must be accessible to employees on the shift, not filed in a manager's office.

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: Adding a product from a different category to the purchase — a case bought with a laptop — while upselling moves the customer up within the same line to a larger or higher-grade version of what they already chose. Suggestive selling covers both from the counter; the line that separates these two is category versus tier.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail roleplays scored on add-on sales ask you to name and demonstrate the technique, and calling a larger size a cross-sell is the error judges catch immediately.

terms.definition: Stated as a share of the selling price rather than in dollars: (price - variable cost) / price, or total contribution / total sales. It converts a dollar sales target straight into profit, and it differs from a gross margin ratio because only genuinely variable costs are subtracted from revenue.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks how much additional revenue is needed to fund a $5,000 promotion is solved by dividing that spend by this ratio, not by the gross margin.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: Accurately modeling what another person is thinking and feeling without necessarily sharing the feeling — perspective-taking. Affective empathy is catching the feeling itself, and compassionate empathy adds the impulse to act; only this first form can be deployed deliberately in a negotiation, and it is the one that can be trained in a session.
terms.whyItMatters: Negotiation and conflict roleplays are graded on stating the other side's reasoning back to them accurately before arguing, which is this and not sympathy.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: Sets the average category buyer's annual purchase volume at 1.00 and states a brand's buyers against it, so 1.30 means the people who choose this brand buy 30% more of the category per year than the typical buyer; it is the third multiplier that converts a penetration figure and a repeat rate into a share estimate.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the factor students silently drop from a share forecast, turning a 12% answer into 10%, and it is the evidence behind a plan that argues for targeting heavy users instead of chasing more triers.

terms.definition: Unpaid media coverage generated through PR, news, and referrals.
terms.whyItMatters: Publicity builds credibility through sources other than paid ads.

terms.definition: Governs contracts for the sale of goods — movable, tangible items — and displaces common-law contract rules for them, so services, employment and real estate stay under common law. Its section 2-207 is the sharpest break: a definite acceptance forms a contract even when it adds terms, where the common-law mirror-image rule would have turned the same reply into a counteroffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam fact patterns about a purchase order with extra terms typed on the back are decided first by asking whether goods or services were sold.

terms.definition: Lifts a mature item's sales by changing who buys it or how often rather than changing the item: volume equals users times usage rate, so new user segments, new uses, and more use per occasion are the three levers; product modification instead alters the item's quality, features, or style.
terms.whyItMatters: Maturity-stage questions ask what a marketer does when sales flatten; the pair of levers must be told apart, since a judge hears 'add a feature' as the other strategy entirely.

terms.definition: Empirical pattern in which roughly the top 20% of a category's buyers generate about 80% of its volume, and the heavier half of buyers accounts for 80% to 90% of units in many packaged-goods categories — so a 10% lift among heavy users is worth several times the same percentage lift among light users, and a promotion measured in customers reached can be worth less than one measured in volume reached.
terms.whyItMatters: Promotion-budget roleplays that ask where to spend a limited fund are won by weighting the target by consumption share rather than by headcount.

terms.definition: An arrangement where the supplier monitors the buyer's usage data and decides replenishment timing and quantity, while the buyer still owns and pays for the stock on hand — consignment differs precisely there: the supplier retains ownership until the item is sold or consumed.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays ask who should hold the replenishment decision and who carries the cash tied up in the stock; the ownership line is what separates the two arrangements.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: Federal postal law lets anyone who receives goods they never ordered keep them as a free gift, with no duty to pay and no duty to ship them back, and a follow-up invoice creates no obligation. Only free samples plainly marked as such and merchandise sent by a charity asking for a donation fall outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal-and-ethical selling items describe a company mailing a product with a bill attached and ask what the recipient owes; a customer-complaint roleplay expects you to tell the caller the item is theirs.

terms.definition: Hofstede's 0-to-100 measure of whether people define themselves as 'I' or as part of a permanent in-group: the United States scores about 91, the highest of the fifty-plus countries surveyed, and Guatemala about 6. It answers a different question than power distance, which measures tolerance of unequal authority, and a country can be strongly collectivist while low in power distance. The communication consequence differs accordingly - a high score licenses naming one person's contribution and negotiating one-to-one, a low score requires the group to settle a position before any single voice states it.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item asking why singling out one employee for praise backfired with an overseas team is scored on this dimension, not on generic 'cultural differences.'

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: Understanding another person's state, being moved enough to care, and then acting to help — the third mode alongside cognitive and affective empathy. It is the form that produces a commitment rather than a mirror, and because it converts feeling into action it avoids the exhaustion that pure affective empathy causes in people who absorb distress all day.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges scoring a supervisor responding to a struggling employee award the answer that names the feeling and then commits to a specific change, not the one that only shares the distress.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: Total marketing spend divided by net sales, times 100 — programs, salaries, agency fees and campaigns, not just media — so it answers what the plan costs to run. Marketing ROI asks the opposite question, what the same spend returned.
terms.whyItMatters: Control questions ask which metric shows a plan is over budget versus which shows it was unprofitable; naming the wrong one loses the item even when the arithmetic is right.

terms.definition: A schedule carrying a low continuous weight all year with heavier bursts layered over the peak selling weeks, so unlike flighting the brand is never entirely off air, and unlike continuity the weekly weight is not flat.
terms.whyItMatters: A client with year-round sales and a holiday spike is the standard prompt for this pattern; naming it and drawing the line against the other two schedules is what separates a scored answer from a vague one.

terms.definition: Matching a checkbook or ledger against a bank statement by adjusting both sides — outstanding checks and deposits in transit on the bank's, fees and interest on the depositor's.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives a statement balance and a book balance and asks for the true cash figure; only adjusting one side gets it wrong.

terms.definition: Promises to repair, replace, or refund a product that fails to meet terms.
terms.whyItMatters: They reduce customer risk and signal confidence in quality.

terms.definition: One brand's sales to a single customer divided by that customer's total category spending over the same period — a household that spends $400 a year on coffee and $120 of it at one chain gives that chain 30% — so it is a per-customer ratio, unlike market share, which divides a brand's sales by the whole category's sales across all buyers; a brand can hold flat market share while its wallet share collapses.
terms.whyItMatters: Customer-relations roleplays that ask how to grow revenue without new customers are answered with this ratio and the cross-sell that raises it.

terms.definition: Recordable injuries and illnesses multiplied by 200,000, divided by total hours worked — the 200,000 representing 100 full-time employees working a 2,000-hour year, which is what makes a small firm's figure comparable with a large one's.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety roleplays give an injury count and an hours-worked total and ask whether the site is above its industry benchmark; a raw injury count cannot be benchmarked and is scored as an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: The reason a customer buys from this particular seller — service, location, reputation, staff knowledge or credit terms — as distinct from the product motive, which is the reason they want the item from anyone at all. A rep losing on patronage grounds cannot recover the sale by describing the product better.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying-behavior exam items sort a list of customer statements into the two motive types, and a roleplay customer who says a competitor is closer to home is testing whether you answer with service instead of features.

terms.definition: Conduct prohibited by the National Labor Relations Act — Section 8(a) lists the five employer violations including interference with organizing, domination of a labor organization, discrimination for union activity and refusal to bargain in good faith, while Section 8(b) lists the union counterparts such as coercion of employees and secondary boycotts. A charge must reach the Board within six months of the conduct under Section 10(b).
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect you to identify which subsection a supervisor's threat falls under during an organizing-campaign roleplay, not merely to call the behavior unfair.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: Creating agreement and buy-in across a group with differing viewpoints.
terms.whyItMatters: It secures team alignment and commitment to shared decisions.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: Scales a controlled market's result to a national number by dividing the test volume by that market's share of national category volume — 60,000 units in a market holding 2% of national volume projects to 3,000,000 units — then discounting for support levels, distribution or pricing that cannot be repeated nationwide.
terms.whyItMatters: Rollout questions give the test units plus the market's percentage of national volume and expect the projection; the discount step is what a judge presses on when a plan's national number looks suspiciously clean.

terms.definition: The channels ads run on — TV, radio, print, digital, outdoor, and social.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right media reaches the target audience cost-effectively.

terms.definition: Freedom from any relationship that would let a firm review its own work: Sarbanes-Oxley bars nine categories of non-audit service for an audit client, forces the lead partner off the engagement after five years, and imposes a one-year cooling-off period before an auditor may join that client as CFO or controller. Objectivity is a mindset; this is the enforceable rule set.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay in which the audit firm is offered the client's bookkeeping work is decided by these prohibitions, not by whether the team feels unbiased.

terms.definition: Puts a written or drawn description of an unbuilt product before target buyers and scores stated purchase intent, normally reading the top two boxes of a 5-point scale -- 'definitely' plus 'probably would buy' -- then discounting that figure, because stated intent runs far above actual trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Feasibility roleplays ask how you would test an idea before building it; naming the intent scale and the discount separates a real answer from 'ask some customers.'

terms.definition: A philosophy that focuses all business activities on satisfying customer needs profitably.
terms.whyItMatters: It reminds competitors that every tactic should trace back to a real customer need.

terms.definition: A formal document requesting goods or services from a vendor at set terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Purchase orders create the paper trail for efficient procurement.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: A selling arrangement in which silence counts as a yes — the seller announces the coming shipment and bills unless the buyer declines in time. It is lawful only if the buyer agreed to the terms up front, gets at least 10 days to reject each announced selection, and can cancel through a route as simple as the one used to enroll.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a book or subscription club and ask what makes the automatic shipment legal; a subscription-selling roleplay is scored on disclosing the cancellation route before the customer signs.

terms.definition: Elkington's reporting frame measuring a firm on three accounts — profit, people, and planet — so that social and environmental results are stated in their own units alongside net income rather than folded into it as goodwill or a marketing expense.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask what a sustainability report adds beyond the income statement, and the answer is the two non-financial accounts named explicitly.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: Bandura's task-specific confidence that you can carry out a particular action, built from four sources in descending order of power — a personal mastery experience, watching a similar person succeed, verbal persuasion, and how one reads one's own physical arousal. Self-esteem, by contrast, is a global judgment of personal worth, so a person can hold high esteem and low efficacy on one specific task.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asking how a manager raises a nervous employee's confidence for a first presentation wants a staged small success rather than a pep talk, since mastery outranks persuasion.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: Averages the size of forecast misses ignoring their direction — the sum of |actual − forecast| ÷ the number of periods — which keeps the error in the product's own units instead of percentages, and roughly 1.25 times this figure approximates one standard deviation of forecast error for setting a buffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecast-error items hand six periods of actuals and forecasts and expect this average computed; it is also the denominator of the tracking signal, so an error here quietly breaks the control check built on top of it.

terms.definition: Media cost divided by impressions delivered and multiplied by 1,000 — a $6,000 magazine page reaching 400,000 readers is $15 — the conversion that makes a cheap small vehicle and an expensive large one directly comparable.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common media-math item on the marketing exam gives two vehicles with different prices and different audiences and asks which is the better buy; the raw price answers nothing and this figure answers it in one step.

terms.definition: A participant that helps goods, money or information move through a channel — a trucking line, public warehouse, bank, insurer or freight forwarder — without ever negotiating terms of sale or taking title. Because it does neither, it adds no channel level, which is why a producer shipping straight to consumers by parcel carrier still has a zero-level channel.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that diagram a channel and ask for its length are scored wrong when the carrier is counted; knowing what these participants do and do not do is the fix.

terms.definition: Laws and rules ensuring fair practices and safeguarding customer rights.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding it helps a business operate ethically and avoid liability.

terms.definition: The percentage of a category's national sales occurring in one market divided by the percentage of the national population living there, multiplied by 100 — a metro holding 2% of the population but 3% of category sales scores 150 — where 100 is exactly average and anything above it means the category is over-developed in that market regardless of how any single brand performs there.
terms.whyItMatters: Media-allocation roleplays ask which markets deserve the spend; the index pair, not gut feel about city size, is what a judge expects to hear.

terms.definition: How many times inventory is sold and replaced over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Turnover reveals inventory efficiency and its impact on cash flow.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: Guidance requiring any material connection between an endorser and a seller — payment, free product, a job, a family tie — to be disclosed clearly and right next to the claim rather than buried in a profile or behind a More link, and requiring a testimonial showing unusual results to state what a typical buyer should expect.
terms.whyItMatters: A social-selling roleplay that has you brief an influencer is graded on where the disclosure sits; exam items ask whether a free product with no cash payment still has to be disclosed, and it does.

terms.definition: Assuming the null hypothesis is true, the chance of observing a result at least as extreme as the one obtained; it is compared with a stated alpha, conventionally 0.05, and the null is rejected only when it falls below, so 0.03 rejects at the 0.05 level but not at 0.01. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that hand you a test result and an alpha are asking whether to reject, and a roleplay judge listens for the comparison to the threshold rather than the phrase statistically significant.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.term: French and Raven's five bases of power
terms.definition: Distinguishes five sources of influence — legitimate power from the position, reward power, coercive power, expert power from demonstrated knowledge, and referent power from personal respect — with the first three attached to the role and the last two to the individual. Expert and referent power produce commitment; coercive power produces compliance only while someone is watching.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking a new team lead with no formal authority to get cooperation is scored on building expert and referent power, and exam items on using power appropriately turn on that split.

terms.definition: The share of a table's rows a filter matches, taken as matching rows over total rows: 200 hits in 100,000 rows is 0.2% and the optimizer uses the index, while a filter matching 40,000 of those rows is unselective and a full scan wins, because chasing 40,000 index pointers back into the table costs more than reading the table once.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asks why adding an index on a two-value status column changed nothing; the fraction of rows matched, not the presence of the index, decides it.

terms.definition: (actual minus planned) / planned x 100, carried on every line of the marketing plan: $92,000 delivered against a $100,000 forecast is -8%. The sign alone does not say good or bad — negative on revenue is unfavorable, negative on expense is favorable.
terms.whyItMatters: Mid-year review items give planned and actual columns and ask which lines need action; competitors who read every negative as a problem flag the underspent line that is actually helping.

terms.definition: What one rating point of a market costs: spot price divided by the program's rating, so a $3,000 spot on a 5-rated program is $600. It prices a percentage of a market where cost per thousand prices raw impressions, which is why it cannot be compared across markets of different sizes.
terms.whyItMatters: Broadcast-buying items ask a competitor to rank stations within one market, where this is the right measure, then ask to compare a small market against a large one, where it is the wrong one and cost per thousand is needed instead.

terms.definition: Setting prices based on what competitors charge for similar products.
terms.whyItMatters: It is essential for positioning and staying competitive.

terms.definition: A pre-release trial run by the developer's own employees inside a controlled company setting, so defects are found before any outsider sees the product; beta testing hands the same build to real customers in their own environment, which makes who runs it and where the dividing line between the two.
terms.whyItMatters: Development-stage exam items list a testing activity and ask which stage it belongs to; the answer turns entirely on whether outsiders are involved.

terms.definition: The bundle of benefits a business promises to deliver to a specific customer group.
terms.whyItMatters: A sharp value proposition anchors positioning, messaging, and pricing.

terms.definition: Inspecting products and services to ensure they meet set standards.
terms.whyItMatters: It catches defects early, protecting satisfaction and reducing waste.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: Months a newly hired rep needs before carrying full quota, credited in steps — commonly no quota in the first quarter, half in the second and full in the third. A rep hired in March therefore contributes roughly a quarter of an annual number that year, which is why headcount added late almost never rescues a current-year gap.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-management items ask what revenue a mid-year hire adds this year, and the credit schedule is the whole answer; a roleplay on onboarding new sellers expects you to name the stepped quota rather than promise full production on day one.

terms.definition: Requires certain agreements to be evidenced by a signed writing before a court will enforce them: sales of land, promises that cannot be performed within one year, promises to answer for another party's debt, agreements made in consideration of marriage, executor promises, and sales of goods priced at $500 or more under UCC section 2-201. A covered oral deal is not void — it is unenforceable if the other side raises the defense.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges ask which handshake commitments a manager can still rely on, and the $500 goods figure and the one-year rule are what settle it.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%. It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: Leading by modeling integrity, fairness, and moral principles.
terms.whyItMatters: It builds organizational trust and sets the tone for employee behavior.
